promise: Introduce charter (partnership) schools
detail: Secured in ACT's 2011 support agreement with National. The enabling Education Amendment Bill was introduced in October 2012 and became law. The first five partnership schools (kura hourua) opened in Auckland and Northland in February 2014. Between 2014 and 2017 the authorisation board approved 17 of 111 applications. The Labour-led government abolished the model in 2018, and all 12 remaining schools became state-integrated or special-character schools by September 2018.

promise: A low, near-flat income tax (about 15%, with the first $25,000 tax-free for people who opt out of state cover)
detail: Never enacted. By 2021 ACT no longer advocated a flat tax, and it campaigned in 2020 and 2023 for lower graduated rates instead (see the 2020 and 2023 tax entries).

promise: Regulatory responsibility / regulatory standards law setting principles for good law-making
made: Long-standing: 2006 member's bill (Hide), 2011 support agreement, 2023 coalition agreement
detail: ACT proposed this for almost two decades. Rodney Hide's 2006 member's bill and the 2011 Regulatory Standards Bill (from the Regulatory Responsibility Taskforce) both failed. It was finally delivered under the 2023 coalition agreement: the Regulatory Standards Bill was introduced on 19 May 2025 and passed its third reading on 13 November 2025, 68–55, with only National, ACT and NZ First in favour. It took effect on 1 January 2026, and the first Regulatory Standards Board members were appointed in April 2026. Public opposition was very strong: the Ministry estimated that 88% of almost 23,000 submissions on the discussion document opposed it, and about 99% of submissions to the select committee were against it. NZ First, which voted for the bill, has since pledged to repeal it.

promise: Three-strikes sentencing for burglary
made: 2014 election (announced by leader Jamie Whyte, March 2014); repeated 2026
detail: Never enacted. The three-strikes regime reinstated in 2024 covers serious violent and sexual offences, not burglary. In July 2026 deputy leader Nicole McKee announced that ACT would again campaign on adding burglary to it.

promise: Review and replace the Resource Management Act
detail: The National-led coalition repealed Labour's replacement laws (the Natural and Built Environment Act and Spatial Planning Act) in December 2023. In September 2026 Parliament passed two replacement laws, the Planning Act 2026 and the Natural Environment Act 2026, sponsored by National's Chris Bishop. ACT's Simon Court served as Parliamentary Under-Secretary for RMA reform. The RMA, as amended, remains the main law during a four-year transition, so the change is legislated but not yet in full effect.

promise: Expand partnership (charter) schools
detail: David Seymour became Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Education Minister with responsibility for charter schools. More schools were approved and opened between 2014 and 2017, and a support entity, E Tipu E Rea, was funded in 2016. All of this was reversed by the incoming Labour-led government in 2017–18.

promise: Legalise assisted dying (End of Life Choice Bill)
detail: Seymour's member's bill passed its third reading in November 2019. To win NZ First's votes, an amendment made the law subject to a binding referendum, which passed 63–57. Voters approved it at the 2020 referendum, and the End of Life Choice Act came into force on 7 November 2021. This was ACT's biggest policy win during its one-MP years (2011–2020).

promise: Permanent income tax cuts, including cutting the 30% middle-income rate to 17.5%
detail: Not delivered during 2020–23, when ACT was in opposition. In 2023 the coalition adopted National's smaller tax-threshold package rather than ACT's rate structure (see the 2023 tax entry).

promise: Abolish 'demographic' ministries: the Ministry for Women, Ministry for Pacific Peoples and Ministry for Ethnic Communities, plus the Human Rights Commission
detail: Not included in the 2023 coalition agreement, and all three ministries still exist with ministers in the National-led government. ACT's 2026 fiscal plan again proposes abolishing 'demographic' ministries.

promise: Abolish the Māori electorates and reduce Parliament from 120 to 100 MPs
detail: Not in the 2023 coalition agreement and not progressed in government.

promise: Referendum on the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi, made a condition of coalition with National
detail: In 2022 ACT said the referendum would be a condition of forming a government with National. It dropped that condition in the 2023 coalition negotiations. Instead, the agreement only committed National to support a Treaty Principles Bill up to and through select committee.

promise: Pass a Treaty Principles Act defining the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi
detail: The narrow coalition commitment was honoured. The bill was introduced in November 2024 and passed its first reading on 14 November 2024, 68–54, with National and NZ First support. That vote prompted the Hīkoi mō te Tiriti. The select committee received about 300,000 written submissions, a record, and around 90% opposed the bill. On 10 April 2025 it was voted down at second reading, 112–11, with only ACT in favour. National and NZ First had said beforehand they would vote against it at that stage. ACT's actual goal, a Treaty Principles law, was therefore not achieved.

promise: A Ministry for Regulation and a Minister for Regulation to cut red tape
detail: The Ministry for Regulation was established on 1 March 2024, funded partly by disestablishing the Productivity Commission, with Seymour as the first Minister for Regulation. It has carried out sector reviews, starting with early childhood education in 2024. It also drew criticism over staff salaries (70 permanent staff averaging about $150,000 in April 2025).

promise: Bring back charter schools and let state schools convert to charter schools
detail: Legislation passed on 25 September 2024. Budget 2024 allocated $153m to convert 35 state schools and open 15 new charter schools in 2025–26 (50 in total). The first seven schools opened in February 2025 and 18 were operating by July 2026, with 1,732 students on 1 July 2026. The first state-school conversion happened only on 12 October 2026. The law is in place, but the scale is well short of the 50-school plan.

promise: Restore interest deductibility for residential landlords, faster than National proposed
detail: Legislated in March 2024: 80% deductibility from 1 April 2024 and 100% from 1 April 2025.

promise: Tenancy law changes including pet bonds
detail: The Residential Tenancies Amendment legislation passed in December 2024. It introduced pet bonds, restored 90-day no-cause terminations and shortened some notice periods. Renters' United criticised the changes.

promise: Reinstate the three-strikes law
detail: The Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act passed on 13 December 2024, introduced by ACT's Nicole McKee, and has applied since 17 June 2025. It covers the same serious violent and sexual offences as the 2010 law plus a new strangulation offence, with changes intended to make it more workable.

promise: Tougher action on gangs (gang patch ban, gang membership as an aggravating factor)
detail: The gang patch ban and the aggravating-factor laws passed on 19 September 2024 with National, ACT and NZ First support. These were National's flagship policies, which ACT backed. Some critics noted a tension with ACT's free-expression principles.

promise: Rewrite the Arms Act 1983 and move the firearms regulator out of Police
detail: Nicole McKee's Arms Bill was introduced in December 2025 and passed its first reading with broad support. It passed its third reading on 29 July 2026 and received Royal assent on 4 August 2026 as the Arms Act 2026, replacing the 1983 Act. The new law sets up a firearms regulator separate from the Police Commissioner, bars gang members from holding licences and gives the regulator infringement powers. Commentators noted the final vote was much less unanimous than the 2019 reforms. Implementation is phased.

promise: Review the firearms registry
detail: The review was in the coalition agreement. In May 2025 ACT invoked the 'agree to disagree' clause after National declined McKee's call for a more 'thorough and independent' review of the registry.

promise: Shrink the public service back to its 2017 size by cutting back-office functions
detail: Thousands of public-sector roles were cut. Reported totals ranged from about 3,745 by May 2024 to over 9,000 by 2025, depending on the source and what was counted. Even so, Public Service Commission data show 63,912 full-time-equivalent staff at 30 June 2026, against 63,117 in June 2023 and a peak of 65,699 in December 2023. The 2017 public service was about 13,000 FTE smaller than in 2022, roughly 47,000. Headcount has not returned to anything near 2017 levels.

promise: Larger, flatter income tax cuts (ACT's tax plan)
detail: The coalition agreement said ACT's flat-tax principles would be 'considered'. What was enacted was National's package: about $14 billion of income tax relief in Budget 2024, worth $4–$40 a fortnight to workers earning over $14,000. ACT's rate structure was not adopted.

promise: 90-day trial periods for all employers
detail: Passed on 21 December 2023 as part of the 100-day plan.

promise: Repeal Fair Pay Agreements
detail: Repealed on 14 December 2023 (a shared National and ACT policy).

promise: Narrow the Reserve Bank's mandate to price stability
detail: The Reserve Bank's dual mandate was removed in December 2023.

promise: Reverse the ban on live animal exports by sea
detail: On 10 March 2026 ACT's Associate Agriculture Minister Andrew Hoggard said he could not get Cabinet agreement and the ban would not be overturned this term. He admitted he had earlier promised legislation by then.

promise: Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and abolish the Climate Change Commission
detail: Not included in the 2023 coalition agreement, and the Act and Commission remain. In August and September 2026 ACT revived both pledges, including scrapping the net-zero target.

promise: Deliver public services based on need, not race
detail: On 13 September 2024 the Cabinet Office directed that public services be delivered on the basis of 'need' rather than 'race', and the target for Māori business procurement was dropped. Te Aka Whai Ora (the Māori Health Authority) was disestablished in 2024. After ACT pressure, ACC's Māori and Pasifika health targets were scrapped in May 2025. Some ethnicity-based programmes remain, and ACT is campaigning in 2026 for further law changes.

promise: Repeal section 7AA (Treaty obligations) of the Oranga Tamariki Act
made: 2023 coalition agreement (ACT's Karen Chhour, Minister for Children)
detail: The repeal passed on 3 April 2025. This was despite a May 2024 Waitangi Tribunal finding that it breached Treaty guarantees and related Court of Appeal litigation.

promise: Make the free school lunch programme cheaper
detail: Associate Education Minister Seymour redesigned the scheme in 2024: bulk-purchased meals for intermediate and secondary students, with a stated saving of about $130m a year. The new supplier model drew widespread complaints about meal quality. Funding was extended for 2027 ($212m), with changes flagged for 2028. Cabinet also dropped the programme's Māori name.

promise: Reform Pharmac to fund more medicines faster and give patients a greater voice
detail: Seymour took ministerial responsibility for Pharmac as Associate Health Minister. His July 2024 letter of expectations told Pharmac to stop considering the Treaty and to involve patient groups more, and one director resigned over it. Budget 2024 added $604m over four years for 54 medicines, including 26 cancer treatments (National's cancer-drug pledge). No structural change to Pharmac's funding model was legislated. ACT's 2026 platform again promises to raise Pharmac's share of the health budget; sources differ on the target (10%, 12% or 13% by 2033).

promise: A four-year parliamentary term, subject to a referendum
detail: The narrow commitment was met: the Term of Parliament (Enabling 4-year Term) bill passed its first reading on 5 March 2025. In February 2026, however, the government decided not to progress it this term, and the planned 2026 referendum was dropped.

promise: Shared deputy prime ministership (Seymour from 31 May 2025)
detail: Seymour took over as Deputy Prime Minister from Winston Peters on 31 May 2025, the first ACT MP to hold the role.

promise: Raise the NZ Super eligibility age by three months a year (with compassionate access for people in physically demanding jobs) and pause Super Fund contributions
detail: Part of ACT's 2026 fiscal plan, alongside returning non-welfare spending to 2017 per-capita levels, $653m of disability-benefit savings and abolishing demographic ministries. National kept the age at 65 under its 2023 deal with NZ First.

promise: Freeze the adult minimum wage for three years and introduce a training wage for under-20s
detail: Announced on 15 September 2026 as part of ACT's small business policy.

promise: Disestablish the Waitangi Tribunal once outstanding historical claims are resolved
detail: Announced on 10 September 2026. It would apply once all claims lodged by 1 September 2008 are resolved.

promise: Tighter immigration rules: deport serious non-citizen offenders, a five-year benefit stand-down for new residents, a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge on temporary work visas, and an end to the permanent resident visa category
detail: Announced on 3 May and 31 August 2026. This is a shift from ACT's 2023 coalition agreement, which leaned towards liberalising some visa settings.

promise: Entrench equal rights, the rule of law and parliamentary sovereignty in the Bill of Rights, Constitution Act and Legislation Act
detail: Announced on 23 August 2026. It continues ACT's 'equal rights' agenda after the Treaty Principles Bill was defeated.
